newsitem.title: UK: Peru's Fujimori says no ransom money available.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori says no ransom money available.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Monday that there was no chance of ransom money being paid to Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
But he said during a visit to London he was still hopeful that preliminary talks starting on Tuesday could lead to a peaceful solution of the 54-day-old siege.

"As a government we don't accept this kind of ransom payment. I think that all governments, not just the Peruvian but around the world, must not accept these kind of crimes and later pay a ransom," Fujimori told BBC radio.

But the president, in London for an investment conference, added: "I think that the way out for the siege is to find out a peaceful solution... Tomorrow, the preliminary conversations will start and then we can see what happens."

Fujimori said on Sunday that Tuesday's talks would involve his chief negotiator, Domingo Palermo, and the deputy leader of the 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, known by his nom de guerre "El Arabe" -- "The Arab".
But Fujimori said he hoped this could lead to talks with the rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.
The MRTA and government have not held face-to-face talks since December 28, when Education Minister Palermo met Cerpa.
That was 11 days after theheavily-armed MRTA rebels stormed the Japanese envoy's residence and seized hundreds of guests attending an embassy cocktail party.

Most of them have been freed, but the rebels are holding on to a group including the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, Peruvian government ministers, Japanese and local businessmen, and Fujimori's brother, Pedro.
Fujimori said he was not considering the use of force. But he said all could change if any of the hostages were harmed.
Asked if he had considered using more force, he said: "No. We are trying to exhaust all means for a peaceful solution.
"Only if there are victims inside the embassy compound, then there may be another type of solution. But fortunately there's not this kind of problem with the hostages."
The rebels' main demand is the release of about 400 jailed comrades -- something that Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, refuses to discuss.
But the Peruvian president has promised Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto he would seek a peaceful outcome.
In an interview with Reuters on Sunday, Fujimori also denied an asylum deal had been set up.
"We haven't had success finding a country where they could seek asylum. It is quite a complex situation and in this moment there are few countries willing to have them," Fujimori said.
Government sources had said Fujimori might travel to Romania after Britain, sparking speculation that the East European country could figure in an asylum deal for the 15 MRTA rebels.
